In agentic RL, expensive GPUs often sit idle waiting on slow rollouts and cheap containers. Nebius’ Di Jin explains how to fix the bottleneck nobody owns.

item.title: “I don’t use Astra every day”: OpenAI developer lead tells TNS why
item.dc:creator: Jennifer Riggins
item.description:
OpenAI’s recent releases have given developers more options for using AI in software. At its 2026 DevDay, the company introduced

The post “I don’t use Astra every day”: OpenAI developer lead tells TNS why appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
OpenAI’s recent releases have given developers more options for using AI in software. At its 2026 DevDay, the company introduced new models, tools, and agents that raise practical questions about cost, speed, safety, and how teams keep up.

On September 29, OpenAI held its fourth annual DevDay near its San Francisco headquarters. The company listed more than 20 major announcements across ChatGPT, Codex, its models, and developer APIs. Among them were GPT-6.1 Sol and a faster Ultrafast tier for GPT-6 Astra; Ultrafast support for Sol followed on October 8.

The announcements included OpenAI dots, persistent agents that can work in the background. Backed by GPT-6 Astra, they can connect to more than 4,000 apps through OpenAI’s plugin ecosystem and take on ongoing responsibilities. 

These agents run continuously in the background, researching and monitoring, then suggesting actions — completing pull requests (PRs), drafting messages, documentation, and analysis, or booking meetings — for human-in-the-loop review. Depending on a user’s rules and the action involved, a dot may proceed, request approval, or leave a sensitive task to the user.

Other updates included the Decisions API, which uses predefined answer choices to classify inputs or route requests, and computer use in the Agents API, which lets agents interact with software interfaces.

Ahead of OpenAI’s Dev Day Exchange on November 3 in London, Vaibhav “VB” Srivastav, OpenAI developer experience and community lead for EMEA, told The New Stack about the cascade of features the company is releasing. The London-based Srivastav also noted how the new releases may affect the day-to-day work of engineers.

This interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.

The New Stack: At DevDay, OpenAI announced more than 20 products and updates. In a time of rapid change, how do developers and engineering managers decide what to use? And how does OpenAI consider the cost of developers absorbing these changes? 

Vaibhav Srivastav: We did ship a lot, right? The overarching goal was to reduce friction for pretty much everyone across the board when we want to release something. This ranges from the average person using ChatGPT to answer questions, to more advanced folks using Codex for day-to-day engineering tasks, to folks in hybrid roles like engineering managers or people managers. From a developer’s lens, I’m particularly passionate about four of those 20 and helped ship them with the team. 

First and foremost is GPT-6.1 Sol. It gets up to 95% of Astra’s performance, but at one-fifth the cost. When we shipped GPT-6 Astra, everyone was like, “Hey, this is a very good model. We love it,” but we couldn’t bring it to a price point everyone could afford for this level of intelligence. That’s why we worked to bring GPT-6.1 Sol to a price point that lets everyone benefit from it across plans.

I don’t use Astra every day. I do use GPT-6.1 Sol as my main go-to.

Sol vs. Astra trade-offs

TNS: OpenAI describes GPT-6.1 Sol as offering “near-Astra intelligence” at one-fifth of Astra’s standard input and output token prices. What type of evaluations back up this idea of ‘near,’ and where does Sol fall short of Astra?

VS: When we get a model, we run traditional benchmarks, including Terminal-Bench 4.0, GDPval, GDP.pdf, SWE-bench, and many others. On those benchmarks, GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Astra are very close. Both Terminal Bench and SWE-Bench are good indicators of how a model would perform on difficult and long-running tasks. In both benchmarks, 6.1 Sol is empirically very close to GPT -6 Astra. 

Second, and more importantly, we dogfood these models internally before they’re ready to ship to see how good a particular model is. A good measure of success is when everyone starts adopting that model as their daily driver across engineering, product, and adjacent teams like marketing, human resources, and so on. When we started dogfooding this model, we saw a rapid increase in people switching to GPT-6.1 Sol as their daily driver.

They could use whatever they want. We have no internal limits on what people can do with these models, so they can choose whichever model they want, and they keep choosing 6.1 Sol.

TNS: For a developer or a team choosing among GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and the Ultrafast speed tier, what’s the decision rule? When is premium worth paying for?

VS: In my opinion, Sol gets you about 95% there for most tasks. For a new project or an unfamiliar problem, I would turn to Astra to look for loopholes or things I may have missed.

“If I use GPT-6.1 Sol to work on that feature and then use the same model for code review, it’s like checking my own work. I’d be biased toward saying it’s good.”

If I use GPT-6.1 Sol to work on that feature and then use the same model for code review, it’s like checking my own work. I’d be biased toward saying it’s good. For an adversarial review, I give GPT-6 Astra fresh context and ask it to poke holes, take the work apart, and help me make sure it’s safe, secure, and gets me the outcome I want.

TNS: Where does Ultrafast mode fit in?

VS: Ultrafast is for important, real-time use cases like fraud detection, financial investigations, and code investigations. Developers have told us they want something extremely fast for those cases. Ultrafast mode lets GPT-6 Astra, and now also GPT-6.1 Sol, deliver remarkably fast outputs — over 300 tokens per second — at a higher price than the standard tier, but still quite affordable. 

We later added 6.1 Sol to Ultrafast. It costs 1.2 times standard Astra, so you get near-Astra performance at more than 300 tokens per second for 20% more than Astra.

Guardrails and Auto-review

TNS: Let’s talk about guardrails both around the plans developers can use, and also around safety and governance. 

VS: Any feature that could add costs for enterprise or business users is off by default. They need to opt in explicitly. 

The more interesting point for me is safety. As models do more and get faster, we want their actions to align with what you want. One of my favorites is called Auto-review. Before the model acts, a Luna-level [lightweight, ultra-efficient] model checks it against a policy you define.

For example: I don’t want the model to submit anything on my behalf, send emails, or share personally identifiable information. An organization or solo developer can define the policy, allowing these models to run safely and autonomously for longer. 

Last week we made Auto-review free for Codex and ChatGPT subscribers — over 5 million weekly active users can benefit. We think it’s important to let these models run safely.

See also: OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Terra worked around restrictions in 29.6% of runs in a controlled test

TNS: Now let’s talk about the development and impact of Decisions API.

VS: The Decisions API came together four or five days before DevDay. A team of four or five people shipped a production-ready API in preview for DevDay, then in beta a couple of days later. The Decisions API is multimodal: it classifies text and images and quickly returns structured output. Traditionally, you’d give an LLM a schema and ask for structured output. Now it’s 10 times faster at the same accuracy and costs $0.10 per million uncached input tokens.

How OpenAI dots work

TNS: Finally, let’s talk about one of the major DevDay announcements: OpenAI dots. 

VS: A dot is a persistent, always-on agent that looks across the tools, plugins, and other surfaces you’ve given it access to. It identifies what needs your attention and orchestrates the work to get it done. 

TNS: How does a dot decide what to act on without being asked, and what does a user see when it’s done something on their behalf?

VS: My dot is connected to Slack, where much of OpenAI’s work happens. It is also connected to my GitHub, where I contribute engineering work, and to my Gmail and calendar. Every so often, my dot looks through my Slack messages, DMs, mentions, mail, and calendar. It brings that information together and surfaces things I haven’t acted on or that it can take off my plate.

My team is spread globally, so someone is working around the clock. My dot could be like: Person X tagged you to review this pull request, or Person Y is waiting for information about upcoming model launches. Previously, I spent the morning sifting through thousands of Slack mentions and threads. I specifically tell my dot: Here’s someone on my team and what she does. When she flags things A, B, or C, make sure I know about it. It keeps gathering more context. It knows I want to respond quickly if my boss messages me, so that goes to the top of my list. If a product I’m working on launches tomorrow or the next day, that’s automatically a high priority.

My dot also looks through my engineering work, including PRs, and might say: This is already approved. You can merge it. Or it might say: I can merge it for you as well. I can say yes on my phone, and it can merge the PR, check that tests pass, and verify it looks right in production.

TNS: Some developers say AI leaves them feeling more isolated. Do you miss the sillier things in Slack, like meme sharing or other ways to bond with your engineers?

VS: I’ve had the opposite reaction. I joined OpenAI in December last year. At the time, models were good but couldn’t reliably do things autonomously for me. Now the models are much better. They can get context from wherever you point them to. Before, I spent a lot of time making sure the model did what it was supposed to, leaving less time to catch up or banter with my team. 

“Every Friday, it checks my calendar and blocks 30 minutes with someone I haven’t spoken to in the past three or four days. If I did it manually, I would never stick to it.”

Now I’m more on top of my work because I’m not spending an hour or two sifting through Gmail and Slack messages. I’ve asked my dot to help me catch up each week with someone on my team I haven’t spoken to in a while. Every Friday, it checks my calendar and blocks 30 minutes with someone I haven’t spoken to in the past three or four days. If I did it manually, I would never stick to it.

TNS: With so many recent updates, different teams will be piloting different features. What should they measure to know if it’s working? What metrics turn out to be misleading?

VS: Every new model should be better overall, based on metrics and what we see internally. But the performance boost varies by use case. 

When we ship a model, test it on an isolated use case — a migration, new product, or monitoring task — and measure the lift. The lift can mean the same outcome at a lower cost or a better result. 

For an organization, the question is how much it’s willing to pay for a given outcome. That’s where the other models in the family come in. We’ve got GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Luna, with others in the pipeline. 

The same goes for features like Ultrafast. Not every problem needs Ultrafast, but you might need it to monitor a major user-impacting migration. That’s where Ultrafast with 6 Astra or 6.1 Sol comes in. 

Put a few problems through that test to see whether the model or feature helps. We do the same internally. We run A/B tests to see how features work for users. We also look at product-market fit for each feature or model.

Model deprecation and migration

TNS: OpenAI has accelerated its model release cycle. What commitments can you make to developers building production-ready systems on these APIs about stability and migration paths?

VS: Stability and the end-user experience are important to us. If you go to status.openai.com, you can see our availability, with four or five nines, which means that we actually take this very seriously.

The way we ship models has changed a lot in the past year. Better models help us build the next generation faster, improving productivity for developers and researchers. 

“Because we ship faster, we don’t deprecate a model until we’re certain the next generation is cheaper and more accurate across the board.”

Back in November of last year, we had GPT-5.1. We’re now at GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol. Because we ship faster, we don’t deprecate a model until we’re certain the next generation is cheaper and more accurate across the board. 

For the API, we give three months’ deprecation notice and a migration path so your workflows can be cheaper and better with the next model.

We still serve GPT-5.5 to API users, even though we’re already at 6.1 Sol.

TNS: How can developers manage that much continuous change and migration? What has to change in the traditional agile software development lifecycle?

VS: We see this internally: you build something, and the next model helps you improve it. It’s always a trade-off. There’s always something you care less about. If I built software to solve a problem within my team, I might not need the best frontier performance. 

But let’s say I’m building something that handles transactions for my users or another product they use directly. Then I’d want the best performance and current state of the art. 

Before AI, teams developed software in sprints toward a launch, then paused new features to fix what was broken. They repeated that cycle over months or quarters. We see the same thing with models. 

A new generation arrives; you sprint to use it, then pause. When another model arrives, you use it to improve security and build better features. I see it as an extension of what developers were already doing.

The post “I don’t use Astra every day”: OpenAI developer lead tells TNS why appeared first on The New Stack.
OpenAI shipped more than 20 DevDay updates. Its EMEA developer lead explains when to pay for Astra, when Sol is enough, and what always-on dots change.

item.title: The hidden failure paths that affect Kubernetes control plane availability
item.dc:creator: Sri Saran Balaji Vellore Rajakumar
item.description:
Kubernetes control planes are designed to contain individual failures, but their availability still depends on how components in the critical

The post The hidden failure paths that affect Kubernetes control plane availability appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Kubernetes control planes are designed to contain individual failures, but their availability still depends on how components in the critical path behave under pressure. At fleet scale, a component does not have to crash to contribute to an outage. A valid mechanism can amplify a local defect through shared metadata, synchronized startup work, or an overly aggressive health check. 

For example, an informer gives a controller a local view of cluster state, letting its workers make progress without repeatedly querying the API server. This is efficient when controllers start independently. When many controllers restart simultaneously across a fleet, rebuilding those views can place significant pressure on the control plane. The informer mechanism itself becomes the amplifier.

“At fleet scale, a component does not have to crash to contribute to an outage. A valid mechanism can amplify a local defect through shared metadata, synchronized startup work, or an overly aggressive health check.”

This article examines three cases. In the first, an extension API server published an invalid schema after a dependency upgrade and blocked clients that had never used its API. In the second, DaemonSet agents restarted across a large fleet, turning routine startup work into a request storm the API server couldn’t absorb. In the third, a deep liveness check on a component in the API request path treated a dependency outage as a process failure and drove repeated restarts while the dependency remained unavailable.

These cases matter for teams running extension APIs, controllers that watch large object collections, and components in the API request path that rely on deep dependency checks.

1. Extension API Servers: How a Dependency Upgrade Broke Unrelated Clients

In one of the cluster, Helm deployments started failing for charts that contained only standard Kubernetes resources. The charts had no relationship to the extension API that caused the failure. Users who had never heard of the extension saw validation errors before their requests reached the API server. The failure path ran through metadata, through a schema document that combined definitions from APIs registered in the cluster.

Understanding why requires knowing how Kubernetes exposes API metadata to clients.

Kubernetes can be extended through aggregated API servers, which add new APIs without modifying the core API server. To users, an aggregated API looks native: it has a group, version, kind, and resource paths, and kubectl accesses it through the cluster’s normal API endpoint. An extension API server generates an OpenAPI schema describing its objects and fields. Clients retrieve this schema to understand and validate resources before sending requests.

OpenAPI v2 and v3

Kubernetes exposes this schema contract in two forms, and the difference determines the blast radius of a broken extension. OpenAPI v2 is a single combined document available at /openapi/v2, containing definitions from the core API server and aggregated extension APIs. OpenAPI v3 separates schemas by API group and version. That separation narrows the impact because clients using a core API don’t need to retrieve every extension’s document.

“The v2 format creates a shared failure domain: an invalid definition from one extension can prevent clients from parsing the document used to validate unrelated resources.”

The v2 format creates a shared failure domain: an invalid definition from one extension can prevent clients from parsing the document used to validate unrelated resources.

Explicit OpenAPI model names

Kubernetes PR #131755 made OpenAPI model names explicit. Before this change, Kubernetes could derive a model name from a Go package path. That made it easy to start with a valid schema, but it also tied published model names to implementation details. Moving code or reorganizing packages could change a name that OpenAPI clients saw. The newer approach lets API authors declare a stable model package, and code generation uses that declared value when building schema definitions and references.

Before the change, a schema could expose a definition derived from the raw Go package path:

{
   "com.example.platform.pkg.apis.metrics.v1.MetricReportSpec": {
     "type": "object"
   }
 }
After the change, once the package declares an OpenAPI model namespace, the same definition uses an explicit, stable name:
{
   "com.example.platform.metrics.v1.MetricReportSpec": {
     "type": "object"
   }
 }

A missing declaration

One extension API server upgraded the Kubernetes API machinery dependency without including the +k8s:openapi-model-package annotation required by the updated model name generation. Its generated code continued to supply raw Go package paths when building schema definitions. Earlier API machinery transformed those paths into OpenAPI-safe names; the newer behavior expects the extension to provide a declared model package. Without that declaration, the extension began publishing raw package paths as OpenAPI model identifiers. Because those paths contain /, they made the resulting schema invalid.

The extension server started successfully and continued serving its API. Process health checks do not validate the OpenAPI document a process publishes. The problem appeared in clients that read OpenAPI v2. Because v2 combines API schemas into one document, an invalid definition from one extension can cause a client to report an error before it sends the requested API call, even when the requested resource belongs to a different API.

Helm’s behavior made this especially visible. Depending on the Helm version, command, and validation settings, Helm retrieves the OpenAPI v2 document before applying a chart. A chart using only ordinary Kubernetes resources can fail because an unrelated aggregated API publishes an invalid schema. Clients using v3 for core resources follow a narrower path: they retrieve the relevant core API document rather than the extension schema that contains the problem.

Test the schema you publish

The most revealing test validates the artifact that clients actually receive. After an upgrade, start the extension and fetch both schema formats:

kubectl get --raw /openapi/v2 > openapi-v2.json
 kubectl get --raw /openapi/v3/apis/<group>/<version> > openapi-v3.json

Parse and validate those documents before enabling the extension in production. Also test with clients that validate requests against the OpenAPI v2 schema. These tests follow the user path and reveal problems that endpoint health checks cannot detect.

2. When a rolling restart becomes a request storm

The cost of rebuilding a local view

A DaemonSet runs one copy of a Pod on every node in a cluster. It suits monitoring, network policy, logging, and security agents that need an up-to-date view of cluster Pods. For example, a network agent may need to map an IP address to its owning Pod for policy or telemetry.

The standard way to maintain that view is through an informer: a client mechanism that lists the required objects and then watches for changes to keep a local cache current.

On a cluster with a few thousand nodes, a cluster-wide Pod informer means a few thousand potential initial list operations. When agents start at different times, the load spreads across the API server’s capacity without incident.

When recovery synchronizes the work

The cost changes when recovery synchronizes the work. In one incident, a DaemonSet ran across thousands of nodes, and its agents repeatedly crashed across much of the fleet. An operator initiated a rolling restart to recover them. The DaemonSet’s maxUnavailable setting seemed protective because it limits how many Pods an update may make unavailable at once.

Those Pods were already unavailable. Their replacements did not necessarily face the same pacing constraints. Many agents started nearly simultaneously.

Each new agent creates its informer. Each informer begins by listing the same collection of Pods. A recovery operation intended to reduce the failure footprint can therefore create a large, synchronized population of requests against the API server.

The cost of a list request

Informers commonly make their initial request with the resourceVersion parameter set to 0. By using 0, the client allows the API server to answer from its watch cache in memory rather than performing a direct read from etcd, the API server’s backend datastore. This is normally the fast path. It avoids repeated storage reads and uses a view of the state the API server has already assembled for watches.

For years, that path had an unintuitive limitation. The watch cache could not provide pagination in the same way that lists served from etcd could. A client could include limit=500 and reasonably believe it had bounded the response to 500 objects. In affected request paths, when the list was served from the watch cache with resourceVersion=0, the API server could ignore the limit and return every matching object. 

On a large cluster, a response containing all Pods may include tens of thousands of objects and occupy hundreds of megabytes while the API server decodes, filters, serializes, and sends it. When thousands of replacement agents request the same full collection together, the server can exhaust available memory and CPU constructing many copies of the same answer. Ordinary control plane traffic then waits.

Reducing the startup load

The Kubernetes community has improved this part of the stack. API Priority and Fairness list-cost estimation was corrected in Kubernetes 1.31. WatchList can also replace the traditional list-then-watch startup path in clients that support it. These improvements reduce the per-request cost, but they do not change the broader design calculation: a cluster-wide informer in a DaemonSet still multiplies its startup cost by the number of nodes, and a retry policy can still synchronize that cost during a failure.

The question for an agent owner is: what is the smallest Kubernetes resource collection this informer can watch and still fulfill its function?

An agent that only needs Pods in one namespace should not list all Pods cluster-wide. An agent that needs Pod metadata should consider a metadata-only informer rather than transferring full Pod specifications. An agent interested in service backends may be able to use EndpointSlices instead of listing every Pod because EndpointSlices describe service endpoints directly and are typically much smaller than the full Pod inventory.

An agent that truly needs Pod-to-IP ownership, labels, or other Pod metadata may still need to watch Pods, but it should restrict that watch to the relevant namespaces, nodes, or labels whenever its semantics allow. The goal is not to eliminate Pod informers. It is to avoid reconstructing more cluster state than the agent can use, especially when recovery causes many instances to start together.

3. When a liveness check restarts what it cannot fix

A liveness probe that checks downstream dependencies will restart a process whenever those dependencies are unavailable. If the process sits in the API request path, each restart can interrupt API traffic. When the dependency outage persists, the probe drives a cycle of restart, initialize, fail dependency check, and restart again. Each iteration adds latency without repairing the dependency.

“The probe may faithfully execute its contract. The contract may still be wrong.”

The probe may faithfully execute its contract. The contract may still be wrong.

Static stability depends on cached key material

Kubernetes control planes may depend on an external Key Management Service, or KMS, to encrypt Secrets. The KMS provider uses that service for key operations, while the API server can retain cached encryption material in memory. That cached state is part of the system’s availability design. A transient loss of KMS connectivity may delay operations that require fresh key material without immediately making the API server unable to serve useful requests.

A Liveness probe that tested the wrong thing

In one incident, an encryption provider that integrated Kubernetes with an external KMS had a liveness probe monitored by the kubelet. The probe performed a fresh encryption operation, followed by a decryption operation, against the external KMS every few seconds. When a network impairment made the KMS endpoint unreachable, the probe failed, and the kubelet restarted the provider. The restarted provider couldn’t establish a new KMS session, so it kept restarting while the dependency remained unavailable.

The probe accurately reported that the KMS endpoint was unreachable. It could not determine whether the provider process could no longer serve its local interface, or whether the API server had exhausted the cached encryption material that let it keep working. Neither conclusion followed from a failed call to the external KMS.

The cascade through API server health

The risk was broader because the API server’s composite /healthz check included the KMS provider’s status. A failed provider could therefore replace an API server with usable cached encryption state. The new API server had no warm encryption cache, needed to establish a new KMS session, and faced the same unreachable dependency. Repeated replacements could turn a transient KMS impairment into a loss of control plane serving capacity.

Preserve capability during an impairment

This is the difference between testing dependencies and testing capabilities. KMS reachability was a useful monitoring signal, but it was not sufficient evidence that either the provider process or the API server had lost all useful capability. The liveness probe should determine whether the provider is stuck or unable to serve its local interface. A separate dependency check can alert operators that KMS is unavailable without automatically triggering a restart.

The same reasoning applies to any component in the control plane path. A cached credential, an established connection, or an in-memory view of state may be the only thing allowing useful work to continue while an upstream service recovers. This behavior is already built into components such as kube-proxy and CoreDNS: kube-proxy continues using its last-known Service and Endpoint state, while CoreDNS continues answering from the Kubernetes data it already has, even when the API server is temporarily unavailable.

“Each case shares a structural property: a mechanism can operate correctly within its own contract yet still violate the availability contract of the system it belongs to. Component-level correctness is necessary but insufficient.”

Restarting every process that cannot reach every dependency discards cached state, increases the amount of state that must be rebuilt, and creates synchronized demand on an already impaired dependency.

Each case shares a structural property: a mechanism can operate correctly within its own contract yet still violate the availability contract of the system it belongs to. Component-level correctness is necessary but insufficient for system availability.

The general design principle is to evaluate every mechanism on the critical path for its behavior when its assumptions are violated. Schema aggregation assumes extensions publish valid schemas. Rolling restart pacing assumes Pods are available to become unavailable. Liveness probes assume restart moves a process closer to health. When those assumptions break, the mechanism can amplify the failure it was designed to contain.

For platform teams operating shared control plane components at scale, these are practical review criteria for upgrades, recovery exercises, and health-check design:

  • Validate the schema artifacts that clients receive, not only the extension process.
  • Limit informer scope and startup work to the smallest resource collection the component requires.
  • Separate dependency monitoring from liveness decisions when a component can retain useful capability during an impairment.
  • Test recovery behavior when many replicas restart simultaneously.

These practices help keep a local failure local, preserve useful capability during dependency outages, and prevent ordinary recovery work from becoming a control plane incident.

For additional resilience guidance, see the Amazon EKS Best Practices Guide.

Learn how valid Kubernetes mechanisms can unintentionally amplify defects, trigger request storms, and break control plane availability.

item.title: When “isolated” doesn’t mean isolated: How to sandbox AI agents
item.dc:creator: Michael Levan
item.description:
Separation of workloads before AI wasn’t easy, but it was far more straightforward. Servers sat in data centers, VLANs segregated

The post When “isolated” doesn’t mean isolated: How to sandbox AI agents appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Separation of workloads before AI wasn’t easy, but it was far more straightforward. Servers sat in data centers, VLANs segregated packets, firewall rules managed ingress/egress, and physical cables separated packets to and from their destinations.

Now, flip on an agent, and it has access to almost everything by default.

Enterprises cannot operate with that default, and in this article, you’ll learn how to implement true sandboxing at every layer that matters.

Why aren’t containers enough to sandbox AI agents?

When you run a container (think Docker), it’s a lightweight package that runs as an isolated process. But that isolation has limits. Containers share the host kernel, and those on Docker’s default bridge can communicate with one another. A container cannot directly access host files by default, but a writable bind mount can let it modify or delete the host files exposed through that mount.

If you rely on a container alone for agent isolation, you may leave important boundaries unprotected. Thinking of containers as locked down by default is a major security risk. When running workloads in Kubernetes, you have tools like NetworkPolicy, service mesh for secure service communication, and SecurityContext to ensure containers run in a governed way.

That’s why having default security out of the box, easily turned on, and policy enforcement built into your AI sandboxing solution is key to enabling all teams. Without it, every organization risks thinking security exists, only to face a harsh reality.

So, regardless of what agentic workloads we’re running, the question we must answer is: “What makes up a true sandbox?”

What’s a true agent sandbox?

OpenAI reported that agents in restricted research sandboxes found a route to the internet through its internal Artifactory service; an agent later found and shared publicly exposed Hugging Face credentials. Anthropic described a different failure: in three cybersecurity evaluations, Claude reached real systems because a third-party test environment had internet access despite instructions that it did not. These cases show that sandboxing depends on the network and service boundaries around an agent, not just the runtime that contains it.

“These cases show that sandboxing depends on the network and service boundaries around an agent, not just the runtime that contains it.”

Agent sandboxing by default can sound “buzzword-ish”, but there is merit in implementing it at all of the boundaries that count for you and your organization. That means sandboxing will look different depending on where, and ultimately how, you put it into production. For example, sandboxing an agent with access to government- or healthcare-related data could mean locking down ingress/egress to public, consumer-based LLMs and allowing the agent to interact only with dedicated models for specific tasks on the data it must use. On the flipside, a software engineer or architect coding up a new integration may have more flexibility in the LLMs, MCP Server tools, and agent skills that agents they’re using can interact with and ultimately where those Agents can run (e.g. on your laptop/desktop vs an isolated server running an Agent runtime).

That’s where the fun, ironic consulting answer of “it depends” comes in, because it really does. As with everything security-related, there is a spectrum of what you can implement ranging from “cover the key use cases” to “this is Area 51”, and that plethora of range needs to be thought about and ultimately implemented in the best and most efficient way for your organization.

So, here’s the answer to the underlying question from this section’s header: true agent sandboxing means clarifying, understanding, and implementing what your agents should and shouldn’t be able to interact with. This includes other agents, LLMs, web searches, MCP servers, tools, and APIs.

“True agent sandboxing means clarifying, understanding, and implementing what your agents should and shouldn’t be able to interact with.”

In the next section, you’ll learn the key differentiating factors that make up a true sandbox. With that knowledge, you’ll be able to draw a proper conclusion about what level of agent sandboxing an organization should implement.

The differentiating factors for your agent sandbox

There are four key areas that you must keep in mind when implementing agentic workloads:

  • Software vs. hardware-level isolation (think user space vs. at the chip level)
  • Where the agents run (is it running on an isolated runtime or your workstation)
  • What the agents have access to (ingress/egress/web search/models/tools/APIs)
  • Secure code execution for AI agents (what commands/code/scripts can an agent run)

When thinking about software-level isolation, think container-level isolation. Now, after the first section of this blog post, ” Why aren’t containers enough to sandbox AI agents?, you may be thinking to yourself, “No way I’m going to run Agents in containers; it’s not isolated at all.” That’s true, but only by default/out of the box. You can secure and govern software-level isolation; it’s just a matter of what policies you put in place to ensure it. It runs inside a Linux kernel using Linux Namespaces/the user space for boundaries. Hardware isolation, on the other hand, is running a guest VM (think microVM/Firecracker) at the chip/CPU level. That means it runs a dedicated, standalone guest VM, and all processes run inside that guest VM.

The next two pieces of the puzzle are where agents run, and that brings us back to the previous section. An agent can run on your laptop/desktop, in a container, or within an isolated guest VM at the hardware level. Regardless of which option you choose, you still need proper guardrails, policy enforcement, and access to LLMs and tools, but the segregation may occur elsewhere. In any case, outbound and inbound connectivity (to/from the agent) occurs at your “line of communication”, which is an AI gateway. That’s typically where you set up policies, guardrails, tool isolation, agent access, and LLM connectivity.

The final step is “how” the agents run. For many use cases, agents run on a laptop/desktop. Still, in an organization, most agentic runtimes run on a server/platform like Kubernetes (which also covers “where” the Agents run). For example, an agent you may interact with on an eCommerce website isn’t running on someone’s laptop; it runs on a hosted runtime.

When working with a hardened solution, the ability to ensure agents run within your harness of choice and that it implements a true agent sandbox environment under the hood should be out of the box, and this is an important decision factor.

kind: Harness
metadata:
  name: YOUR_HARNESS_NAME
  namespace: YOUR_NAMESPACE
spec:
  kagent: {}
  workload:
    image: YOUR_AGENTIC_WORKLOAD_IMAGE
  substrate:
    workerPoolRef:
      name: kagent-default
    snapshotPolicy:
      location: ACTOR_SNAPSHOT_STORAGE_LOCATION
  allowedAgentTemplates:
    selector:
      matchLabels:
        kagent.dev/harness: kagent

kind: AgentTemplate
metadata:
  name: assistant
  namespace: kagent
  labels:
    kagent.dev/harness: kagent
spec:
  modelConfig:
    name: default-model-config
  description: A substrate-backed assistant used to verify this main build.
  systemPrompt: You are a helpful assistant running on agentic workloads.

Choosing the right agentic runtime, and therefore framework, lets you specify which AI gateway your agent traffic goes through from the sandbox, which harness you use, your underlying software- or hardware-level isolation, governance around agentic workloads, and where agents store memory/context.

Closing thoughts

Sandboxing agents will always come down to a keen understanding of what those AI agents need to do, and that’s the hardest part. Locking down an agent and implementing governance, security, and policy enforcement should be easy with the right tooling and platforms. The “what” is crucial. What exactly are you locking down and why?

The post When “isolated” doesn’t mean isolated: How to sandbox AI agents appeared first on The New Stack.
Containers alone cannot secure AI agents. Discover how to build true sandboxing across hardware, software, and network boundaries.

item.title: One pod, one node: The architecture behind serverless Kubernetes on AWS
item.dc:creator: Sri Saran Balaji Vellore Rajakumar
item.description:
A pod-level walkthrough of admission routing, dedicated scheduling, and network isolation, no worker nodes required Serverless Kubernetes changes who manages

The post One pod, one node: The architecture behind serverless Kubernetes on AWS appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
A pod-level walkthrough of admission routing, dedicated scheduling, and network isolation, no worker nodes required

Serverless Kubernetes changes who manages the node, not what Kubernetes expects from it. Kubernetes expects a node to register with the control plane, report capacity, run a Kubelet, provide networking, and host workloads. AWS Fargate provides those behaviors without asking customers to create, patch, scale, or replace a fleet of worker nodes.

Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) Fargate solves that problem by making the pod the unit of infrastructure. When a pod is selected for Fargate, EKS provisions a dedicated compute environment, boots the Kubernetes components it needs, gives the pod an Elastic Network Interface (ENI) in the customer’s virtual private cloud (VPC), and tears the environment down when the pod is gone.

“Serverless Kubernetes changes who manages the node, not what Kubernetes expects from it.”

That customer experience depends on several coordinated design choices. Admission-time routing prevents the default scheduler from claiming a Fargate pod. A Fargate-specific scheduler provisions capacity instead of selecting from a pre-existing node pool. A focused runtime image supplies the Kubernetes node components, while separate network namespaces keep the platform path distinct from the workload path. An admission handler on the node limits workloads to patterns that fit a one-pod, one-environment model.

This article follows the components that make pod provisioning possible, from admission and scheduling through the node runtime and networking.

Routing a pod before scheduling

An EKS cluster can use nodes from Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) and Fargate at the same time. Placement therefore needs to be explicit before the ordinary scheduling flow begins.

EKS provides a Fargate profile, an AWS resource that indicates which pods run on Fargate. A profile expresses that intent by selecting a namespace and, optionally, pod labels. It also specifies the private subnet and security group used for the pod’s Elastic Network Interface, so placement and network access are chosen together.

For clusters with Fargate enabled, AWS manages and operates an admission webhook as part of the Kubernetes control plane. When a pod matches a profile, the mutating webhook adds the matching profile’s name to the pod’s label. It also sets the pod’s scheduler name to the Fargate scheduler, so the pod follows the Fargate scheduling path. This decision happens before the pod object is persisted in the Kubernetes database (etcd) and before the default scheduler can claim it.

A profile also specifies the pod execution role, an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role used by the Fargate infrastructure to register its kubelet and pull images from Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR). That role is distinct from the application identity containers use. Because this is a serverless infrastructure, EC2 instance metadata is not available to Fargate pods, so applications that call AWS services should use IAM roles for service accounts.

Provisioning a node for the pod

The Fargate scheduler is a dedicated scheduler that runs on the Kubernetes control plane. It requests new capacity for a pod based on the pod’s resource requirements and its matching Fargate profile, rather than searching a pool of existing nodes.

“The Fargate scheduler is a dedicated scheduler that runs on the Kubernetes control plane. It requests new capacity for a pod rather than searching a pool of existing nodes.”

Once capacity is requested, the scheduler tentatively associates the pod with a nominated node. This prevents a retry or resync from provisioning a second environment for the same pod. The Fargate runtime registers the Kubernetes Node object when the environment is ready, and the scheduler performs the final bind after the node reports ready. The runtime then starts the pod and reports its status through the API server.

When the pod terminates, the runtime removes the node and releases its capacity. If provisioning or binding fails, reconciliation clears the tentative assignment and reclaims the capacity before retrying.

One pod, one network interface

Fargate connects each pod to the customer’s VPC through its ENI. The Fargate profile defines the private subnet and security group used for that interface. Security-group rules and VPC routing therefore apply to the pod’s ENI rather than to a shared customer-managed worker node.

An ENI gives the pod a first-class place in the VPC. VPC flow logs can identify the interface, and security-group rules can express the intended workload boundary.

The network path has to serve two audiences at once. The Fargate platform needs a path for managed telemetry, credentials, and provisioning. Kubernetes components need a path to the API server, and the customer pod needs a path to the VPC. Fargate keeps these paths connected where Kubernetes requires them while separating platform traffic from workload traffic.

Fargate provisions three logical Linux network namespaces. The platform namespace carries the Fargate platform services, including telemetry, credential vending, and provisioning. The node namespace carries the Kubernetes core data-plane components and customer ENI. The workload namespace runs the customer workload. The underlying Fargate implementation can change, but this separation keeps the managed platform, Kubernetes node components, and workload on distinct paths.

The customer ENI is moved into the node namespace, where it provides the path for Kubernetes control-plane communication and pod traffic. The task metadata endpoint is reachable from the node namespace, allowing the node runtime’s AWS authentication path to obtain the credentials needed to register the node with the API server, while access from the workload namespace is blocked. A bridge and virtual Ethernet (veth) pair created by the Container Network Interface (CNI) connect the node namespace to the workload namespace. The node namespace handles traffic destined for Kubernetes management endpoints; all other traffic is delivered to the workload namespace and exits through the customer ENI. Filtering prevents the pod from reaching platform metadata and management processes.

The runtime image is a Kubernetes node in miniature

The runtime image matches the Kubernetes control-plane version, so the kubelet and its supporting components remain compatible. It provides the kubelet and Kubernetes node components needed to register the node, receive pod specifications, start and restart containers, run probes, report status, and serve operations such as logs and exec.

During kubelet startup validation, the default scheduler can place a pod before the Fargate kubelet completes initialization. EKS runs a custom PodAdmitHandler that validates a pod before it starts and admits only a pod intended for the Fargate scheduling path. This protects the one-pod-per-node model when another pod is observed while the kubelet is coming up and provides a second validation boundary after API-server admission.

The managed kubelet does not need every capability available on a general-purpose node. Kubernetes provides controls to disable the logs, profiling, and debug-flags handlers, and EKS uses them to keep the runtime surface limited to the operations the service needs. We contributed some of these controls upstream through changes that disable the logs handler and changes that disable profiling and debug flags.

Fargate patching and considerations

Fargate’s managed runtime is maintained continuously, and EKS periodically replaces Fargate pods so they receive the latest available security patch without customer-managed node operations. When a Fargate environment needs patching, EKS identifies the affected pod, notifies the customer, and uses the Kubernetes Eviction API to gracefully remove the pod before recycling the environment. For controller-managed workloads, this gives a replacement pod an opportunity to become ready before the old environment is retired.

A customer’s PodDisruptionBudget controls how much application capacity can be unavailable during that process. EKS respects the budget when it requests eviction and retries when eviction would violate it. The budget must leave room for planned disruption; if eviction still cannot succeed by the scheduled termination time, EKS can eventually delete the pod so it can create the patched environment. Replicas and readiness probes determine whether the application continues serving traffic.

Customers must design around this independent pod lifecycle. Every pod must match a Fargate profile.

Customers should plan ENI and subnet capacity accordingly. A design that works on EC2 because many pods share a node’s interface must account for one ENI per Fargate pod. Fargate profiles use private subnets, and Fargate pods are not assigned public IP addresses. Internet or AWS-service access normally uses the private subnet’s network address translation (NAT) gateway or VPC endpoint design. Because the customer ENI carries both Kubernetes data-plane and pod traffic, its security group must allow the Kubernetes management traffic needed for operations such as kubectl logs and kubectl exec.

A workload contract that fits the model

Most Kubernetes application workloads fit naturally on Fargate, including Deployments, Jobs, and multi-tenant applications whose isolation boundary is the pod. Workloads that require node-level control, such as DaemonSets, host networking, host ports, privileged operations, or GPUs, fall outside the Fargate pod contract and require an execution model that provides node-level access.

Storage follows the same boundary. HostPath and host-attached block storage depend on a persistent node, and Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) cannot be mounted to Fargate pods. For durable shared file storage, Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) is the supported pattern. For supported Kubernetes features, read the current EKS Fargate documentation.

“Making Kubernetes serverless required more than hiding the worker node. EKS had to preserve Kubernetes behaviors while changing the underlying lifecycle.”

Making Kubernetes serverless required more than hiding the worker node. EKS had to preserve Kubernetes behaviors while changing the underlying lifecycle. Admission establishes placement intent before schedulers compete. A scheduler provisions capacity and waits for a node to prove readiness. Runtime components supply the node contract, while node-level admission protects the pod boundary. VPC networking gives each pod a direct, controllable identity, while namespace and VM boundaries keep the managed platform separate from the workload.

These decisions are mostly invisible when they work. A deployment selects a profile, a pod starts with the expected VPC access, logs and exec behave like Kubernetes operations, and the underlying environment disappears when the workload is gone.

That invisibility is the point of the service. Customers can use familiar Kubernetes objects and workflows while EKS and Fargate absorb the work of provisioning, isolation, node lifecycle, and runtime maintenance. The infrastructure is managed, but the contract remains Kubernetes: a pod is admitted, scheduled, connected, and observed as a first-class workload.

The post One pod, one node: The architecture behind serverless Kubernetes on AWS appeared first on The New Stack.
Discover how AWS EKS Fargate executes serverless Kubernetes with dedicated pod scheduling, custom runtimes, and isolated VPC networking.

item.title: OpenAI halved its agent’s price. Its own safety report flagged a catch.
item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell
item.description:
OpenAI launched GPT-6.1 Terra on Monday, cutting API prices in half and delivering major gains in coding and computer-use benchmarks.

The post OpenAI halved its agent’s price. Its own safety report flagged a catch. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
OpenAI launched GPT-6.1 Terra on Monday, cutting API prices in half and delivering major gains in coding and computer-use benchmarks. But the company’s own safety tests reveal a catch. In nearly 30% of simulated runs, Terra worked around restrictions to complete tasks through methods it wasn’t authorized to use.

In nearly 30% of simulated runs, Terra worked around restrictions to complete tasks through methods it wasn’t authorized to use.

The system card also shows Terra taking unauthorized actions in 13.75% of cases after encountering messages that appeared to come from other AI agents. Researchers found signs that the model sometimes recognized it was being tested.

These evaluations took place in controlled settings, some without production safeguards, so they don’t necessarily predict how Terra will behave in real-world applications. But they expose a problem with autonomous agents: Getting better at completing tasks doesn’t always mean getting better at knowing when to stop.

Cheaper, faster, better at coding

OpenAI is pitching Terra as a cheaper way to run coding agents and automate computer tasks, with substantial performance gains over its predecessor.

On Terminal-Bench 4.0, Terra solved 50.3% of problems at maximum reasoning effort, compared with 21.5% for GPT-5.6 Terra. OpenAI says GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Astra remain better choices for the toughest coding work.

Price may be the bigger selling point with $1 per million input tokens and $5 per million output tokens through the API; half the standard price of GPT-5.6 Terra and GPT-6.1 Sol.

The model is available through the OpenAI API as gpt-6.1-terra, as well as ChatGPT Work and Codex for Plus, Pro, Enterprise, and Edu users.

When agents ignore the rules

OpenAI’s “Respecting Warnings” evaluation tests whether models honor access-denied errors and other restrictions while carrying out legitimate tasks in simulated professional environments. At maximum reasoning effort, Terra found ways around those restrictions in 29.6% of runs. This was more often than GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6 Luna, and GPT-6.1 Sol, but less often than GPT-6 Sol.

OpenAI also recently updated the evaluation to count successful workarounds, meaning a more capable model could score worse simply because it’s better at finding alternative routes, not necessarily because it’s more willing to break the rules. The tests were also conducted mostly in low-stakes scenarios without system-level safeguards.

Across 48,701 shared tasks, Terra showed signs of recognizing it was being tested in 9.88% of trajectories, compared with 4.35% for GPT-6.1 Sol and 8.07% for GPT-6 Astra.

Across 48,701 shared tasks, Terra showed signs of recognizing it was being tested in 9.88% of trajectories, compared with 4.35% for GPT-6.1 Sol and 8.07% for GPT-6 Astra. That doesn’t mean Terra deliberately tried to game the tests, but it makes its behavior harder to interpret. An agent needs to distinguish between a malicious instruction and a legitimate restriction, but when it gets it wrong, it may cross boundaries it was supposed to respect.

Messages from other agents

A separate evaluation tested how models respond to messages that appear to come from other AI agents. Across 80 samples covering 10 scenarios, Terra attempted to communicate with apparent peers in 65% of cases. In 11 cases, or 13.75%, it performed the specified unauthorized action, compared with 1.25% for GPT-6.1 Sol and 16.25% for GPT-6 Sol.

OpenAI cautions against treating the difference as a straightforward regression. Much of it involved promises of future assistance that Terra indicated it would not actually carry out. The company considers Terra’s overall performance on this measure comparable to GPT-6 Sol.

Critical cyber at a discount

Even at a lower price, the company classifies GPT-6.1 Terra as having Critical cybersecurity capability under its Preparedness Framework. The threshold covers capabilities such as independently developing functional zero-day exploits against hardened systems or carrying out sophisticated cyberattacks from high-level instructions.

On OpenAI’s internal port of ExploitBench, Terra achieved a 24.5% success rate developing arbitrary-code-execution exploits for recently disclosed vulnerabilities.

GPT-6.1 Sol scored 21.5%, while GPT-6 Astra reached 31.5%. On Sandbox Bench, which tests vulnerabilities in runtimes, file parsers, and egress proxies, Terra succeeded against five of 22 targets. GPT-6.1 Sol succeeded against nine and GPT-6 Astra against 10.

The company acknowledges that Terra still struggles to reliably exploit recently disclosed vulnerabilities. Even so, its performance shows that cutting inference costs doesn’t necessarily mean sacrificing offensive cybersecurity capability.

Lower prices could make legitimate vulnerability research more accessible, while also making safeguards against misuse more important. OpenAI says Terra receives the same cybersecurity protections used for GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol, adjusted for the new model.

Not every safety test tells the same story

In one evaluation, Terra made no attempts to bypass Codex’s Auto-review system, which uses a separate model to block unsafe commands outside a sandbox.

A larger simulation of 48,690 internal Codex tasks produced 22 flags for serious misaligned behavior, or 0.045% of tasks. GPT-6.1 Sol received 24 flags, GPT-6 Astra received 26, GPT-6 Sol received 38, and GPT-5.6 Sol received 61.

OpenAI defines these incidents as actions a reasonable user wouldn’t expect and would strongly object to. The findings came from simulated tasks, not confirmed incidents in real-world deployments. Terra also demonstrated resistance to prompt-injection attacks comparable to GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol. Despite the flagged behavior, OpenAI determined that the model’s safeguards were sufficient for public release.

Despite the flagged behavior, OpenAI determined that the model’s safeguards were sufficient for public release.

item.title: AI is changing Kubernetes; is your platform ready for 2027?
item.dc:creator: Nick Lucchesi
item.description:
AI workloads, including those using agentic AI, will only add to and change the questions Kubernetes teams have to answer. It’s no longer

The post AI is changing Kubernetes; is your platform ready for 2027? appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
AI workloads, including those using agentic AI, will only add to and change the questions Kubernetes teams have to answer. It’s no longer merely enough to ask if the pods are running. Or how long it takes a model to produce its first token. Or what happens when inference traffic spikes and no additional GPU capacity is available.

Increasingly, questions like those are becoming platform questions that sit next to the already familiar work of upgrades, recovery, and security.

That’s why The New Stack has just published Kubernetes in 2027: Building Platforms for AI, Autonomy, and Scale, a new ebook by Chris J. Preimesberger, in partnership with HPE.

This ebook starts with the work before launch — before the launch. We ask teams to stress-test model-serving systems under realistic loads, rehearse failures, and measure more than GPU utilization.

It also takes a clear-eyed look at agents. Giving an agent access to a cluster is a consequential decision, even if its task sounds routine.

The guide calls for identifiable owners, narrow permissions, approval gates, and audit trails that connect tool calls to the task that prompted them. It asks teams to evaluate AI output quality. A fast answer offers little comfort when it’s wrong.

And the ebook doesn’t treat AI as a reason to forget the rest of the platform. The checkpoints cover policy across clusters, visibility into services outside Kubernetes, upgrade and restoration drills, operational ownership, and developer self-service.

The checklist gets specific about the work that can fall between teams.

Can you see which clusters follow a shared access and network baseline? (And who approved the exceptions?)

Also: When an application slows, can you look beyond pod metrics to the database, virtual machine, network, or external service it depends on? Before the next upgrade, have you checked for removed APIs and practiced restoring both cluster state and application data?

Then there’s the work after deployment: Who renews an ingress certificate? Who signs off on a capacity change? If a developer requests an environment through a service catalog, does it come with an owner, a review date, and a way to see what it costs?

They’re practical prompts for conversations among platform teams, application teams, security teams, and business teams. Download the ebook now before you start the conversation.

The New Stack has launched a new ebook, sponsored by HPE, with 10 practical checks for Kubernetes platforms handling AI workloads and agents.

item.title: Most of Anthropic’s Q3 revenue came from models that barely existed six months ago
item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell
item.description:
Anthropic’s long-awaited S-1, filed Monday ahead of its planned Nasdaq debut under the ticker ANT, shows how quickly customers are

The post Most of Anthropic’s Q3 revenue came from models that barely existed six months ago appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Anthropic’s long-awaited S-1, filed Monday ahead of its planned Nasdaq debut under the ticker ANT, shows how quickly customers are spending on its newest models.

According to the filing, models released in the six months leading up to September 30 accounted for more than 80% of the company’s third-quarter revenue. Anthropic released eight widely available Claude models between April and September 2026, plus three restricted-access Mythos models. The filing doesn’t say how much revenue each generated; models launched in late September had only days to contribute to the quarter.

But that raises an interesting question for developers: Are newer models delivering better results for developers’ tasks, and what do those results cost?

Are newer models delivering better results for developers’ tasks, and what do those results cost?

How new models compound

The filing suggests there’s a reason newer models account for so much of Anthropic’s revenue. The company says customer spending is closely tied to how often it releases new models and what those models can do. Each improvement naturally gives customers more reasons to use Claude, while more capable models attract new customers and encourage existing ones to use Claude more and spend more in the process.

That spending helps fund the next round of development. Anthropic says in the filing that the company relies on growing revenue to pay for the research, computing power, and technical talent needed to build more capable models. Those improvements can then attract more customers and drive additional spending, creating a cycle in which each generation of Claude helps fund the next.

Improvements can then attract more customers and drive additional spending, creating a cycle in which each generation of Claude helps fund the next.

Did demand drive releases?

The filing shows how important newer models are to Anthropic’s revenue, but it doesn’t establish whether customer demand has influenced the company’s faster release schedule in 2026. While the two may be connected, Anthropic doesn’t say that increased spending is what drove it to release models more frequently.

Revenue, not customer migration

The 80% figure also doesn’t tell us how many customers switched to newer models. A relatively small group of customers spending heavily on the latest releases could account for much of that revenue.

The filing offers some context for how much spending can vary. Anthropic’s heaviest Claude Code enterprise users spend roughly 20 times more than other enterprise users. That doesn’t tell us which models they’re using, but it shows why revenue alone can’t tell us how many customers have made the switch.

Choosing the newest model

Developers building coding agents, retrieval pipelines and automation tools may default to the most powerful model without first checking whether a smaller or cheaper alternative could handle the job. That spending adds up. Reuters reported — citing attendees at Anthropic’s October 14 investor meeting — that the company generated $16.8 billion in third-quarter revenue.

Anthropic reportedly generated $16.8 billion in third-quarter revenue.

Whether developers actually need the latest models or simply prefer them, Anthropic benefits from the spending. With models released since April accounting for more than 80% of its third-quarter revenue, Anthropic has a strong financial incentive to keep improving Claude.

Anthropic has also called for pacing frontier AI development so safety work can keep up with growing model capabilities. The filing does not show whether commercial demand has affected that approach.

Anthropic’s S-1 reveals models under six months old drove over 80% of Q3 revenue, sharpening a debate about developers’ pull to the newest models.

item.title: Ex-GitHub CEO launches a GitHub rival that reinvents the pull request
item.dc:creator: Frederic Lardinois
item.description:
Entire, the startup founded by former GitHub CEO Thomas Dohmke, on Monday launched its GitHub alternative that replaces the traditional

The post Ex-GitHub CEO launches a GitHub rival that reinvents the pull request appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Entire, the startup founded by former GitHub CEO Thomas Dohmke, on Monday launched its GitHub alternative that replaces the traditional pull request model with a new agentic code review system called Trails.

The company has been launching parts of its platform since it announced a $60 million seed round in February. Early on, Dohmke occasionally noted he wasn’t planning to compete with GitHub.

But with Monday’s launch, Entire is launching a full GitHub alternative, with its own twist on what a modern GitHub for the agentic era should look like.

At launch, Entire supports native hosting for private repositories. Public repositories and self-hosted Git nodes are still on the roadmap.

“It’s the moment we’ve been waiting for,” Dohmke told The New Stack last week during an interview at the Linux Foundation’s AGNTCon + MCPcon in San Jose, California. “It’s exciting for us because what we set out to do a year ago is landing now — and bringing the Git hosting and the infrastructure layer together, with sites around the world, […] and the idea of continuous integration, continuous delivery, continuous memory, and then with Trails, our reinvention of the pull request.”

“It’s exciting for us because what we set out to do a year ago is landing now.”

Entire, like other devtools startups, argues that the new bottleneck for developers isn’t writing the code — agents take care of that — but code review. Unlike some other startups in this space, the company isn’t solely focused on that. Instead, the Entire is betting that solving the code review bottleneck requires an entirely new platform.

In his keynote at AGNTCon + MCPcon, Dohmke described a review queue growing in two directions: agents producing more changes, and those changes containing more code.

“I open a pull request, and I realize I have no idea what all that code does,” he says of his previous experience using coding agents.

Right now, that platform consists of Entire’s Git-compatible server, the continuous memory feature for agents that the company originally launched with, and Trails.

From pull requests to Trails

Trails is Entire’s take on the pull request model, but instead of developers reviewing code changes manually, Trails gives them a dashboard with customizable evals scored by agents. That system may assess how risky a code change is, for example, or how much intent drift has occurred over a long LLM-driven development session.

Entire says those evals run on every push, with findings available through both its web interface and its open-source CLI. Coding agents can then use that feedback to address problems and push another revision, while the developer validates the progress.

In the end, the original request, the agent’s session history, and the resulting code all become part of the review.

GitHub already offers agentic code review through Copilot. Entire’s pitch goes beyond adding an AI reviewer to a pull request: It makes the intent behind a change and the agent’s work part of the review process alongside the code.

For Entire, the idea here is that if the evals come back green, it’s ok to merge the code without a detailed human review (though few human code reviews are probably as detailed as they should be).

By default, Entire provides preset review agents, but developers can also define their own configurations in a JSON file and choose among supported Claude and OpenAI models.

“We’re redefining how the developer lifecycle works, and it’s really cool. I’ve been at home in the evenings, sitting on my couch, and texting my agents — all the while getting links from my team to their Trails on Slack and opening them.”

“We’re redefining how the developer lifecycle works, and it’s really cool,” Dohmke says. “I’ve been at home in the evenings, sitting on my couch, and texting my agents — all the while getting links from my team to their Trails on Slack and opening them. And because the user interface is designed for seeing — we’re calling it the head-up display for the pilots– so I look at my head-up display, and I see the ‘stop cop,’ one of the evals that we have internally, and if that’s green and the confidence is high, then we’re merging it.”

Entire is also partnering with Buildkite and Depot for CI. Developers can convert their existing GitHub Actions workflows using Buildkite’s bk pipeline or Depot CI, then connect the repository in Entire.

A faster, distributed Git forge

While Trails is the headline news here, Entire’s core is its Git-compatible distributed source control server, which debuted earlier this summer.

Entire says it can push up to 89x faster than GitHub and 6x faster than Cursor’s Origin.

But while a distributed system with mirrors across geographic regions helps, the key feature for many corporate users may be that Entire was built from the outset to offer private repositories in specific regions, too. Given today’s data governance landscape, that’s an increasingly important feature.

The available regions include the U.S., Europe, India, and Australia. Dohmke says customers choose a primary region and can add mirrors elsewhere, with Entire handling synchronization between them.

Memory for agents

Continuous Memory is Entire’s third pillar. It syncs AI agent sessions into a project’s repository and makes that available to the agents for future use.

For Dohmke, those sessions also preserve the approaches a developer rejected and the moments when they told an agent that working code still wasn’t what they wanted.

The company says the system combines a codebase graph that helps agents find relevant code with an “agentic brain” that turns previous sessions and prompts into memories they can query. That lets agents retrieve earlier decisions and the context behind them when they start another task.

Dohmke expects agent run costs to become the next bottleneck, with teams paying closer attention to token efficiency alongside engineering productivity. He argues that developers may find it’s cheaper to use an existing open-source project or a service like Entire than to spend tokens generating their own replacement.

The platform is free; however, Dohmke says customers pay only for the tokens the review agents consume.

But because these review agents run on LLMs, they still cost money. Right now, Dohmke says, Entire is giving all its users a $100 starter credit. Once users have run out of these credits, they will pay market rates for the model of their choosing.

The arbitrage between the discounts it can get and that market rate seems to be Entire’s current business model.

GitHub has always had very generous plans for open-source projects, and its maintainers and Dohmke hinted that the company may offer help there as well, noting that Entire is already working with some partners, including model vendors, on ideas. “More to come,” he says.

Also of note: Entire’s announcements on Monday come two days before the 2026 edition of GitHub Universe, the company’s flagship developer event in San Francisco. What timing.

The post Ex-GitHub CEO launches a GitHub rival that reinvents the pull request appeared first on The New Stack.
Ex-GitHub CEO Thomas Dohmke’s startup Entire launches a GitHub alternative that swaps pull requests for Trails, an eval-driven agentic code review system.

item.title: Claude Code’s top enterprise users outspend other Claude users 20 to 1, Anthropic’s IPO filing says
item.dc:creator: Matthew Burns
item.description:
Anthropic’s IPO filing makes Claude Code the center of its enterprise growth story. The company on Monday filed to go

The post Claude Code’s top enterprise users outspend other Claude users 20 to 1, Anthropic’s IPO filing says appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Anthropic’s IPO filing makes Claude Code the center of its enterprise growth story. The company on Monday filed to go public on Nasdaq. Its S-1 says the average Claude Enterprise user without Claude Code spent less than $75 a month in the third quarter. The top 5% of Claude Code users on Enterprise spent about 20 times that.

Anthropic’s S-1 prospectus spells out a classic land-and-expand play, with Claude Code doing the landing. An engineer picks up Claude Code, likes it, and starts pushing it internally. Anthropic’s sales team show up later, and by then, the filing says, “Claude is often already in use.”

Anthropic calls Claude Code “the product we believe has most concretely defined what autonomous AI work looks like”

Anthropic calls Claude Code “the product we believe has most concretely defined what autonomous AI work looks like” and says non-technical teams are adopting it too. That’s wild for a tool that started in the terminal.

The revenue lines up with that story: Anthropic says it had more than 11,900 customers paying $100,000 or more over the trailing 12 months as of September 30, 2026, up from more than 950 a year earlier. Revenue hit $16.3 billion in the first half of 2026, up from $1.2 billion in the same stretch of 2025. Token usage accounted for 50% of that.

Anthropic’s own engineers? Claude wrote more than 90% of the contributions to the company’s codebase in September, according to the filing.

Anthropic also says the average engineer produced more than 45 times as much code per day in the third quarter as in 2024. Anthropic

Anthropic also says the average engineer produced more than 45 times as much code per day in the third quarter as in 2024. Anthropic says its engineers increasingly direct and review Claude’s work, though it doesn’t define “contributions” or say how much human review that code gets.

I’ve been building one project a week with Claude Code, and I hardly know what I’m doing. The potential velocity is very real.

The S-1 also explains why Anthropic cares about Claude Code beyond coding. The company sells the software that runs Claude Code to other developers.

“A model alone is not an agent,” the S-1 says. Developers can run Anthropic’s harness on their own servers through the Agent SDK, or pay Anthropic to run it as Claude Managed Agents.

That puts Anthropic closer to the companies building coding agents on top of its models. TNS covered how GitHub and Anthropic used their own agents for major Rust rewrites with very different playbooks, and how AWS open-sourced an agent it says is 45% cheaper than Claude Code and Codex.

The S-1 names Google and OpenAI as Anthropic’s primary competitors in frontier models.

The S-1 names Google and OpenAI as Anthropic’s primary competitors in frontier models. Cursor, Replit, and Cognition don’t appear in it.

In its risk factors, Anthropic lists Claude Code among the critical tools in its own development work, so problems with the product “could directly impair our ability to develop and deploy future models.”

It also warns that as Claude takes on more engineering and research, the company “may lose visibility across certain processes in a way that may become difficult for any individual or group of humans to understand and control.”

That sits alongside Anthropic’s public call to pace the frontier, a stance Dario Amodei says may have cost the company an AI lead.

Anthropic plans to list on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT. The filing doesn’t include a price range.
